examples.en: On Memorial Day I visited the national cemetery.
The national cemetery is a quiet and solemn place.
Many people visit the national cemetery every year.
We went on a school field trip to the national cemetery.
I took off my hat in front of the national cemetery.
The national cemetery is not far from my house.

explain: 나라를 위해 일한 분들을 모신 곳이에요. '현충원'이라는 이름으로도 많이 불러요. 장소 이름이라 조용히 하고 예의를 지켜야 해요.

phrases.en: I visited the national cemetery with my family.
phrases.nuance_ko: '가다'보다 일부러 방문한다는 느낌이 있어서 이런 장소에 잘 어울려요.
phrases.nuance_en: Sounds more like a deliberate visit than 'go', which suits a place like this.

phrases.en: You have to be quiet at the national cemetery.
phrases.nuance_ko: 그곳에서 지킬 예의를 말할 때 '에서는'을 붙여 써요.
phrases.nuance_en: Used with '에서는' when talking about manners to keep in that place.

phrases.en: I laid flowers at the national cemetery.
phrases.nuance_ko: '국립묘지'를 다르게 부르는 이름이에요. 이름이 붙은 곳을 말할 때 많이 써요.
phrases.nuance_en: Another name for the national cemetery, often used for the named sites.

explain_en: It is a place that honors people who served the nation. It is also commonly called '현충원'. Since it is a solemn site, visitors should be quiet and respectful.

examples.en: Our house is next to the school.
Which countries neighbor Korea?
I live in a neighborhood next to the market.
The two cities are adjacent, so they are close.

examples.ko: 두 학교가 이웃했을 때는 같이 행사를 했어요.
examples.en: When the two schools were next to each other, they held events together.
If an apartment is next to a park, the air is good.

explain: '이웃하다'는 '~와/과 이웃하다'나 '이웃한 ~'처럼 두 곳이 가깝게 붙어 있을 때 써요. 사람이 옆집에 산다고 말할 때는 '이웃에 살다'나 '옆집에 살다'가 더 자연스러워요. 'ㅎ' 때문에 [이우타다]로 소리 나요.

phrases.en: I live in a city next to Seoul.
phrases.nuance_ko: 바로 옆에 붙어 있는 곳을 꾸며 줄 때 써요.
phrases.nuance_en: Used to describe a place right next to another.

phrases.en: The two countries neighbor each other.
phrases.nuance_ko: 두 곳이 가까이 붙어 있다고 말할 때 써요.
phrases.nuance_en: Used to say two places are right beside each other.

phrases.en: These two cities are not next to each other.
phrases.nuance_ko: 붙어 있지 않을 때 쓰는 부정형이에요.
phrases.nuance_en: The negative form for places that aren't adjacent.

explain_en: 이웃하다 is used in forms like '~와/과 이웃하다' or '이웃한 ~' when two places lie close together. For a person living next door, 이웃에 살다 or 옆집에 살다 sounds more natural. Because of ㅎ, it is pronounced [이우타다].

en: to be located; to be situated

examples.en: A small pond sits in the middle of the park.
An old church stood on top of the hill.

examples.ko: 마을 입구에 큰 나무가 자리한 모습이 예뻐요.
examples.en: The sight of the big tree at the village entrance is pretty.
That cafe is at the end of the alley.

examples.ko: 강 옆에 자리한 집에서 살고 싶어요.
examples.en: I want to live in a house by the river.

examples.ko: 그 식당은 시장 안쪽에 자리하고 있어서 찾기 어려워요.
examples.en: That restaurant is deep inside the market, so it is hard to find.

explain: '위치하다'와 거의 같고, '있다'보다 글이나 안내문 같은 느낌이에요. 여행 소개, 뉴스에서 '~에 자리한 ~'처럼 뒤의 말을 꾸미는 모양으로 자주 나와요. 주어는 보통 건물, 가게, 장소예요.

phrases.example: 그때 들은 말이 아직도 제 마음속에 자리하고 있어요.
phrases.nuance_ko: 장소가 아니라 기억이나 감정이 마음에 남아 있다는 뜻으로 써요. 글이나 노래 가사에서 자주 나와요.
phrases.nuance_en: Used not for a place but for a memory or feeling that stays inside you. Common in writing and song lyrics.
phrases.en_equiv: to live on in one's heart

explain_en: It is nearly the same as '위치하다' and sounds more like writing or signage than plain '있다'. It often appears in travel guides and news in the modifying form '~에 자리한 ~' (the ~ located at ~). The subject is usually a building, shop or place.

dis.h: sit or stand in a place; descriptive

p.n: 소재하다 is more formal and sounds like an official document.

examples.en: Lots of cars pass along this road.

examples.ko: 아침마다 이 골목을 지나다니는 사람이 많아요.
examples.en: Many people pass through this alley every morning.

examples.ko: 매일 그 가게 앞을 지나다녔는데 몰랐어요.
examples.en: I passed by that shop every day but never noticed it.

examples.ko: 버스가 자주 지나다니는 길이라서 좀 시끄러워요.
examples.en: It is a road buses often pass along, so it is a bit noisy.
Drive slowly where children walk by.
I heard that long ago cows used to pass along this road.

explain: '지나가다'는 한 번 지나가는 것이고, '지나다니다'는 같은 곳을 자주 오가는 느낌이에요. '길을 지나다니다'나 '이 길로 지나다니다'처럼 써요.

phrases.en: There are many people passing by in front of the school.
phrases.nuance_en: The verb turned into a modifier describing people.

phrases.example: 어릴 때 이 길을 매일 지나다녔어요.
phrases.en: When I was young, I passed along this road every day.
phrases.nuance_ko: 과거에 자주 오간 일을 말할 때 써요.
phrases.nuance_en: Used for something you did often in the past.

phrases.example: 공사 중이니까 이 길로 지나다니지 마세요.
phrases.en: There is construction, so please don't walk along this road.
phrases.nuance_ko: 그곳을 오가지 말라고 부탁할 때 써요.
phrases.nuance_en: Used to politely ask someone not to go back and forth there.

explain_en: '지나가다' is passing once, while '지나다니다' means going back and forth past the same place often. You can say '길을 지나다니다' or '이 길로 지나다니다'.

examples.en: At low tide I picked up shells at the beachside.

examples.ko: 저녁 바람을 맞으며 해변가를 따라 천천히 걸었어요.
examples.en: I walked slowly along the beachside in the evening breeze.

examples.ko: 이 동네 해변가에 예쁜 카페가 많아요.
examples.en: There are many pretty cafés along the beach in this town.
In summer the children play happily at the beachside.
For this vacation I booked a place to stay by the beach.
I watched the sun rise at the beachside.

explain: '해변'만 써도 같은 곳을 말해요. '해변'에 '가'가 또 붙어 뜻이 겹치지만 말할 때는 자주 써요. 바닷가는 '바닷가에서 살다'처럼 사는 곳에도 쓰고, 해변은 놀러 가는 모래사장 느낌이 더 강해요.

phrases.en: I took photos on the beach.
phrases.nuance_ko: '해변가'와 거의 같고 더 짧게 많이 써요.
phrases.nuance_en: Almost the same as 해변가 but shorter and more common.

phrases.en: There is a small house by the sea.
phrases.nuance_ko: 놀러 가는 곳뿐 아니라 사는 곳도 말할 수 있어요.
phrases.nuance_en: Can refer to a place where you live, not only a place to visit.

phrases.en: I drink coffee at a beachside cafe.
phrases.nuance_ko: 바다 옆에 있는 가게를 말할 때 써요.
phrases.nuance_en: Used for a shop located next to the sea.

explain_en: Just '해변' can refer to the same place. 해변가 adds '가' (edge) to 해변, so the meaning overlaps, but people say it a lot in speech. '바닷가' also works for where people live ('바닷가에서 살다'), while 해변 feels more like a sandy beach for leisure.
